 Social Security COLA history includes 10 of the largest raises since 1975, from 14.3% for 1980 to 8.7% for 2023 and two 5.9% adjustments
 1 / 12 List slides 10 of the biggest Social Security raises since automatic COLAs began in 1975 List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 4, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Across five decades, the yearly raise for Social Security beneficiaries has ranged from 14.3% to nothing at all. That raise is the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. It sets how much benefit checks grow from one year to the next.
 The automatic version of that raise traces back to the 1972 Social Security amendments. Those amendments linked future benefit increases to inflation. The first automatic COLA came with the 1975 adjustment, at 8.0%. Every COLA since then has been tied to the same price measure.
 That measure is the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, usually shortened to CPI-W. When the prices it tracks rise quickly, the COLA rises with them. When prices barely move, the raise shrinks. In some years there is no raise at all.
 This list covers 10 of the largest automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026, ordered from biggest to smallest. The 1977 and 2022 adjustments tied at 5.9%, and each gets its own entry. The 5.8% COLA for 2009 ranks 11th and falls just outside the selection.
 The selection clusters heavily in one period. Every year from 1975 through 1982 appears, accounting for eight of the 10 entries. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% remains the largest of the automatic era, followed by 11.2% in 1981 and 9.9% in 1979. The other two entries are far more recent: 8.7% for 2023 and 5.9% for 2022.
 Each of those recent raises was the largest in decades. The 2023 COLA was the largest since 1981, and the 2022 COLA was the largest since 1982. The adjustments that followed were smaller: 3.2% for 2024, 2.5% for 2025 and 2.8% for 2026. Beneficiaries received no COLA at all in 2010, 2011 or 2016.
 The 2027 COLA has not been announced. This list stops at 2026. For readers tracing Social Security COLA history, the slides that follow place each of these 10 raises in that record.
 1980: a 14.3% COLA, the largest since automatic adjustments began 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1980 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 14.3%. That is the largest automatic COLA from 1975 through 2026, and no adjustment in the decades since has matched it.
 That puts 1980 at the center of a three-year stretch, 1979 through 1981, that produced the three largest automatic COLAs since 1975.
 The gap between first and second place is wide. The 1980 figure topped the next-largest automatic COLA, for 1981, by 3.1 percentage points.
 Only two automatic COLAs have reached double digits, and they came in back-to-back years. The 1980 adjustment is the higher of the pair.
 No other pair of neighboring entries on this list sits that far apart. The rest of the selection steps down in much smaller increments, most of them a percentage point or less. The 1980 raise was more than twice the size of the 5.9% COLAs for 1977 and 2022, the smallest entries in this selection.
 A COLA is a percentage, so its effect scales with the size of each check. Every beneficiary received the same 14.3% increase. A larger benefit therefore grew by a larger amount in dollars.
 Every later COLA was applied to benefit levels that already included the 1980 raise, so the increase compounded over time.
 The 1980 raise also far exceeded the adjustment that launched the automatic system. It came in 6.3 percentage points above the first automatic COLA, for 1975.
 The modern era has not come near it. The 2023 COLA, the largest raise of recent decades, still fell 5.6 percentage points short of the 1980 mark.
 More recent adjustments leave an even wider gap. The 1980 COLA was larger than the 2024, 2025 and 2026 adjustments added together.
 It was also more than double the 2009 COLA, which ranks just outside this selection of the largest automatic raises.
 1981: an 11.2% cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1981 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 11.2%, the second-largest automatic COLA since the mechanism began in 1975. Only the 1980 adjustment was bigger.
 The two years ran back to back. Together they account for the only double-digit raises from 1975 through 2026. Every other automatic adjustment in that span stayed below 10%.
 The 1981 figure came in 3.1 percentage points below the 1980 COLA. It still exceeded every adjustment that followed it.
 The steeper drop came a year later. The COLA for 1982 was 7.4%, a fall of 3.8 percentage points from 1981. That one-year decline was larger than the gap between the 1980 and 1981 raises.
 The 1981 number later became the yardstick for a large modern raise. The 8.7% COLA for 2023 came closer to it than any adjustment since. It still fell 2.5 percentage points short. The two raises sit 42 years apart.
 The 1982 raise arrived just one year after the 1981 COLA. Even so, it missed the 1981 figure by a wider margin than the 2023 adjustment did.
 The 1981 adjustment closed out the double-digit years of the automatic era. No COLA since has reached 10%.
 1979: a 9.9% benefit increase for Social Security recipients 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1979 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 9.9%. It ranks third among automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026, behind only the 1980 and 1981 adjustments.
 The 1979 COLA fell 0.1 percentage point short of double digits. It is the only one of the top three that stayed below 10%. The two adjustments that followed both cleared that mark.
 Together, 1979, 1980 and 1981 hold the top three places in the automatic era. They are the only years since 1975 with a COLA above 9%. They also ran back to back, with 1979 as the first of the three.
 When the 1979 COLA arrived, it was the largest automatic adjustment yet. It was bigger than every raise before it, including the 1975 adjustment that launched the automatic system. It held that position for only a year. The 1980 COLA then surpassed it, and the 1981 COLA followed close behind.
 In size, the 1979 raise sits nearer to 1981 than 1981 sits to the 1980 peak. The largest single jump in the run came between 1979 and 1980.
 The 1979 figure also marked a break from the years just before it. The 1976 COLA was 6.4%. The 1977 COLA was 5.9%. The 1978 COLA was 6.5%. For three straight years, the adjustment stayed within a band of 0.6 percentage point.
 The 1979 adjustment then landed 3.4 percentage points above the 1978 figure. That made it roughly one and a half times the size of the raise a year earlier.
 The 1979 COLA was also 2.5 percentage points larger than the 7.4% COLA for 1982, the year after the three-year run ended.
 No COLA after 1981 has reached the 1979 level. The closest later adjustment, for 2023, sits 1.2 percentage points below it. It was four percentage points larger than the 2022 COLA. The 2026 COLA was less than a third of the 1979 increase.
 2023: an 8.7% COLA, the biggest Social Security raise since 1981 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 2023 cost-of-living adjustment lifted Social Security benefits by 8.7%. That made it the largest automatic increase since 1981, when the COLA reached 11.2%.
 Those two adjustments sit 42 years apart. No COLA from 1982 through 2022 matched or exceeded 8.7%.
 Among all automatic COLAs since 1975, the 2023 increase ranks fourth. Only the adjustments for 1980, 1981 and 1979 were larger. Those three came in consecutive years. That leaves 2023 as the only one of the four largest COLAs from outside that stretch.
 The 2023 raise also topped the first automatic COLA. It finished 0.7 percentage points ahead of the 8.0% adjustment for 1975.
 It still fell well short of the peak years. The 2023 figure trailed 1981's 11.2% by 2.5 percentage points. It sat 5.6 points below the 14.3% for 1980, the largest of the automatic era.
 The 2023 adjustment is also the only COLA after 1982 to exceed 6%. Every other automatic COLA above that level came between 1975 and 1982. That put benefit growth back in a range not seen since the early years of the automatic system.
 The 2023 increase followed a 5.9% COLA for 2022. The step from 5.9% to 8.7% added 2.8 percentage points in a single year. Each COLA applies to the benefit amount already in place. That means the 2023 raise built on checks that had already grown by 5.9% the year before.
 Back-to-back large COLAs also appeared in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The 2022 and 2023 pair is the only consecutive set in this selection from after 1982.
 The Bureau of Labor Statistics produces the CPI-W, the price measure behind the 2023 figure.
 The next adjustment was far smaller. The 2024 COLA came in 5.5 percentage points below the 2023 figure. Through 2026, no later adjustment has come close to 8.7%. It remains the most recent entry in this list.
 1975: 8.0%, the first automatic Social Security COLA 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1975 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 8.0%. It was the first automatic COLA, and it ranks fifth among the largest automatic adjustments from 1975 through 2026.
 That debut grew out of the 1972 Social Security amendments. Before then, benefit increases came only when Congress passed a law. The amendments set up annual raises that would take effect without a new vote each year. The 1975 adjustment was the first one delivered under that system.
 Only four automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026 topped that first raise. Three of them came in a back-to-back run for 1979, 1980 and 1981. The fourth was the 2023 COLA, which beat the 1975 figure by 0.7 percentage point.
 The distance to the very top is much larger. The 1980 COLA came in 6.3 percentage points above the 1975 raise. That made it nearly 1.8 times the size of the first automatic adjustment.
 Most adjustments in the mechanism's first eight years came in below the 1975 raise. The 1976, 1977 and 1978 COLAs each landed below 7%. None came within one percentage point of the 1975 figure.
 The 1982 COLA came closest among those lower years. It reached 7.4%, finishing 0.6 percentage point short of the 1975 mark. That gap is the smallest between the first automatic COLA and any adjustment ranked below it on this list.
 Measured against the modern era, the 1975 raise still sits near the top. Only the 2023 COLA has exceeded it since 1981. The 1975 adjustment topped the 2022 COLA by 2.1 percentage points. It also beat the 2009 adjustment, which falls just outside this selection, by 2.2 percentage points.
 Recent raises fall well below that starting point. None of the COLAs for 2024, 2025 or 2026 reached half of the 1975 figure. Half of 8.0% is 4.0%.
 1982: a 7.4% Social Security cost-of-living raise 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1982 COLA raised Social Security benefits by 7.4%. It ranks sixth among the largest automatic adjustments since they began in 1975.
 That rate stood as a high mark for decades. No later COLA matched or passed it until 2023.
 The 1982 increase closed a four-year stretch in which every automatic COLA came in at 7.4% or higher. That stretch began with the 1979 adjustment. It peaked with the 1980 adjustment, the largest of the automatic era.
 Within that stretch, 1982 was the smallest raise. It was 3.8 percentage points below the 1981 COLA. It was also a little more than half the size of the 1980 adjustment.
 The step down did not mean benefits stopped growing. A 7.4% COLA still raised benefits. The change was in pace: beneficiaries received a smaller raise than in each of the three years before.
 Among the early automatic COLAs in this selection, 1982 sits in the middle. It came in 0.6 percentage points below the first automatic COLA, for 1975. It topped the 1978 adjustment by 0.9 percentage points.
 The years after 1982 look very different. No COLA from 1983 through 2021 made this selection. Even the 2009 raise, the largest in that long gap, stayed below the 1982 rate.
 Before 2023, the 2022 adjustment came closest to the 1982 rate. It still fell 1.5 percentage points short.
 The 2023 COLA was the first to pass the 1982 rate. It beat that rate by 1.3 percentage points.
 Recent raises sit far below the 1982 level. Each COLA from 2024 through 2026 was less than half the 1982 rate.
 1978: a 6.5% inflation adjustment to Social Security checks 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1978 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 6.5%. It ranks seventh among the 10 automatic COLAs in this selection, just ahead of 1976's 6.4% and behind 1982's 7.4%.
 The gap below it is narrow. Only 0.1 percentage points separate the 1978 and 1976 raises. The gap above is wider, at 0.9 percentage points to the 1982 COLA. The 1978 figure was also 1.5 percentage points below the first automatic COLA, 8.0% for 1975.
 The figure came from a formula, not a vote in Congress. Like every automatic COLA since 1975, it tracked the CPI-W, a consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes that index.
 The 6.5% applied as a percentage, not a flat amount. Each beneficiary's monthly benefit rose by the same share. A retiree with a larger check therefore received a larger dollar increase than one with a smaller check. The relative gain was identical for both.
 The raise also applied on top of benefits that earlier automatic COLAs had already lifted. In practice, the 1978 increase built on the 1975, 1976 and 1977 adjustments rather than replacing them.
 The 1978 COLA also broke a pattern. The 1976 and 1977 adjustments had each come in smaller than the year before. At 6.5%, the 1978 raise was 0.6 percentage points higher than 1977's 5.9%. It was the first automatic COLA to exceed the one before it.
 Larger increases followed immediately. The 1979 COLA reached 9.9%, 3.4 percentage points above 1978. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% was more than double the 1978 figure.
 The 1978 raise outranks the 2022 COLA, which matched 1977 at 5.9%. It sits 0.7 percentage points above the 5.8% COLA for 2009, which narrowly missed this selection. Of the two modern raises on this list, only the 8.7% COLA for 2023 was larger, by 2.2 percentage points. The 2026 COLA, at 2.8%, was less than half of 1978's figure.
 1976: a 6.4% COLA in the second year of automatic increases 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1976 Social Security COLA raised benefits by 6.4%. It was the second automatic cost-of-living adjustment, arriving one year after the 8.0% increase that launched the system.
 It was also the first time the automatic raise came in smaller than the one before it. The 1976 increase landed 1.6 percentage points below the 1975 COLA. That drop showed the automatic formula could deliver a smaller raise as well as a larger one.
 The decline continued for one more year. The 1977 adjustment fell another half a percentage point, to 5.9%. That left the 1976 raise in the middle of a three-year slide.
 The direction reversed after that. The 1978 COLA of 6.5% edged past the 1976 figure by a tenth of a percentage point. Then 1979 brought a 9.9% raise, 3.5 percentage points above the 1976 level.
 The first four automatic COLAs stayed within a narrow band. From 1975 through 1978, every adjustment fell between 5.9% and 8.0%. The 1976 raise sat in the lower half of that range.
 The larger raises came later. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% was 7.9 percentage points higher than the 1976 increase. That made the 1980 raise more than twice the 1976 figure.
 Among the 10 adjustments in this selection, the 1976 COLA ranks eighth. It trails seven larger raises and finishes ahead of only the 1977 and 2022 adjustments. The lower end of the list is tightly packed. The gap between the seventh-place 1978 COLA and the two 5.9% raises at the bottom is smaller than the drop from 1975 to 1976 alone.
 From 1983 through 2026, only one automatic COLA topped 6.4%. That was the 8.7% adjustment for 2023. The 5.9% COLA for 2022 fell short of the 1976 level by half a percentage point.
 Recent adjustments have run lower. The 1976 figure is exactly twice the 3.2% COLA for 2024. It is 3.9 percentage points above the 2.5% raise for 2025 and 3.6 points above the 2.8% raise for 2026.
 1977: a 5.9% Social Security COLA that 2022 later matched 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 1977 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 5.9%. That figure ties 1977 with 2022 among the largest automatic COLAs since the mechanism began in 1975.
 The 1977 raise was the third automatic COLA. It followed 8.0% for 1975 and 6.4% for 1976. The adjustment for 1978 then rose to 6.5%.
 That makes 1977 the smallest increase of the first four automatic years. It came in 2.1 percentage points below the 1975 raise. It trailed 1976 by 0.5 percentage point and 1978 by 0.6 percentage point.
 Those figures show a short dip rather than a lasting turn. The COLA eased for two years, bottomed out at 5.9% and then started climbing again. Within two more years, it had reached 9.9% for 1979.
 The 1977 adjustment was also the lowest of the eight straight years from 1975 through 1982. Every other COLA in that stretch was at least 6.4%.
 The two 5.9% years sit 45 years apart, and they arrived from opposite directions. In 1977, 5.9% was a low point inside a run of large raises. The double-digit COLAs for 1980 and 1981 were still ahead.
 In 2022, the same percentage marked a high point instead. It came after 39 straight years, from 1983 through 2021, in which no COLA reached 5.9%. The raise that set the floor of the early automatic era stood above every COLA paid in those 39 years.
 The 2009 COLA came closest to joining the tie. At 5.8%, it fell 0.1 percentage point short of the level shared by 1977 and 2022. COLAs are stated to one decimal place. That means 2009 missed the tie by the smallest margin the published figures can show.
 Both 5.9% years trail the 14.3% COLA for 1980 by 8.4 percentage points. A 5.9% raise is less than half the size of that peak.
 2022: a 5.9% COLA, the largest Social Security raise since 1982 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The 2022 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 5.9%, the largest automatic raise since the 7.4% COLA for 1982. It came 40 years after that 1982 raise.
 The 2022 figure sits 1.5 percentage points below the 1982 raise. From 1983 through 2021, Social Security had 39 annual adjustment years. Every adjustment in that span came in below 5.9%.
 The closest was the 2009 COLA of 5.8%. It fell 0.1 percentage point short of the 2022 figure. Three years in the same span produced no increase at all: 2010, 2011 and 2016.
 Each COLA tracks inflation as measured by the CPI-W. A 5.9% adjustment therefore reflected faster growth in that index than any adjustment year from 1983 through 2021 had shown.
 The 2022 raise matched the 1977 COLA exactly. That tie links one of the earliest automatic adjustments with one of the most recent. The two raises are 45 years apart. They share the lowest spot in this selection of 10.
 The 2022 adjustment held the post-1982 high mark for only one year. The next COLA, for 2023, was 8.7%. That made 2022 and 2023 back-to-back raises above 5%. The 2022 figure was 2.8 percentage points smaller than the 2023 increase.
 The three adjustments after 2023 were all smaller than the 2022 raise. The 2024 COLA came in 2.7 percentage points lower. The 2025 COLA was 3.4 points lower. The 2026 COLA was 3.1 points lower.
 The 2022 raise is also smaller than the peaks of the early automatic era. The 1980 COLA, the largest since automatic increases began in 1975, was 8.4 percentage points larger. The 1981 COLA was 5.3 points larger, and the 1979 COLA was 4.0 points larger. The first automatic COLA, for 1975, also topped the 2022 figure by 2.1 points. The 1982 COLA was itself the smallest of the three adjustments from 1980 through 1982.
